# Research question and hypothesis

I work with the replication package of Rainero, Stolz and Luijkx (2026),
"The Faith Factor" (<https://osf.io/vcxnk/>). The authors measure
researchers' religiosity with a single 0–8 score built from eight items
about belief, practice, and self-identification. They then show that more
religious authors are less likely to support secularization, both in their
personal opinion and in the conclusions of their papers.

A single score assumes all eight items measure the same thing. I test that
assumption. I split the score into two subscales — belief and practice —
and ask which of the two drives the effect.

My question: does the effect run through doctrinal belief or through
religious practice? My hypothesis is that the composite score hides two
distinct axes, and I check whether belief and practice have different
effects on the two outcomes (personal opinion and publication conclusion).
Because I work with already-collected data, my sample is the sample of the
original study.

# Data source and survey design

The data come from an online survey distributed to researchers by email,
self-administered. A second dataset — a hand-coded set of publications by
the same authors — is attached to it. Fieldwork ran from 30 April to
8 June 2021. The replication package with data and code is public on OSF,
so I can pull the original variables and rebuild the analysis.

# Population and sampling

The population is researchers who published on secularization between 2011
and 2020. This is not a random sample from a pre-defined list. It is closer
to a census of an identified population: the authors collected everyone
they could find through a bibliographic search and invited each of them.
The sampling type is closer to exhaustive selection from a bibliographic
database with subsequent self-selection at the response stage.

My reflection: for a question about bias among scholars, this approach is
justified, since the target is a narrow professional community and it is
easier to enumerate than to build a probability sample. The limitation is
that the population is defined through publications — through the output of
activity, not through a list of people. Anyone who did not publish an
indexed article with the right keyword in that window is out, even if they
actively work on the topic. Findings generalise to authors of
secularization articles in WoS for that decade, and beyond that only with
caution.

# Sampling frame

The frame is the Web of Science Core Collection. The authors pulled all
English-language articles with *secularization* or *secularisation* in the
title, abstract, author keywords, or automatic key terms. In February 2021
the search returned 1,664 articles and 2,015 authors and co-authors, with
metadata including email and affiliation.

Two clear distortions in the frame. First, English only. Researchers
publishing in other languages drop out, which systematically shifts the
composition toward Western academia — the authors acknowledge this.
Second, publication type: WoS indexes journal articles above all, while in
the sociology of religion major statements often appear as books. Key
figures like Berger, Taylor, or Casanova are known primarily through books,
and the frame partially loses them as authors. For my question this
matters, because the belief–practice fusion I find may be a property of the
Western journal segment rather than of all researchers of religion.

# Data collection procedure

Of the 2,015 authors found, the contact list was cleaned: 13 duplicates,
22 deceased authors, and 33 people whose email could not be found were
removed. That left 1,947 invitees. The survey was completed by 954 people,
a 49 per cent response rate. Of those, 111 who answered "no" to the filter
question "Is religion one of your research interests?" were excluded, along
with 42 who dropped out on the first page. That left 801 researchers. Their
secularization publications — 1,076 articles in total — were downloaded and
hand-coded by two coders. After excluding irrelevant and inaccessible
papers, the final dataset contains 949 articles by 703 authors.

The procedure is transparent and well documented. A 49 per cent response
rate for an academic survey is high. The weak point is the manual coding of
publications, since deciding whether an article supports secularization
requires judgement, especially in mixed cases. The authors are aware of
this: they set explicit rules and checked inter-coder agreement, with
Cohen's kappa of 0.65 and 83.8 per cent agreement. This counts as
substantial agreement, but not perfect, and some contested articles may
have been classified differently.

# Sample quality: precision, bias, non-response

**Precision.** The dataset is large — 703 authors and 949 articles — and
the WoS metadata are consistent, which gives decent precision for estimates
inside the identified population.

**Bias and non-response.** Half of the invitees did not respond, and
non-response is a problem if it correlates with religiosity itself, which
is exactly what the survey measures. The authors note that belief and
practice questions are sensitive and produce elevated non-response in
academia because of the tension between science and faith. Religiosity
items are missing for 15.8 per cent of cases, and those missings sit on the
sensitive questions. It is plausible that religious researchers in secular
departments respond less often or skip those items, which is a mechanism
that depends on the value of the variable itself — closer to non-ignorable
missingness.

The authors impute missings using multiple imputation with PMM, which
assumes the missingness is explainable by observed variables. If
missingness is tied to an unobserved level of religiosity, that assumption
breaks and imputation does not fully solve the problem. In my analysis I
work on complete cases and do not impute. A useful next step would be an
analysis of non-response itself, for example comparing respondents and
non-respondents on available metadata such as discipline, country, or
productivity, to gauge the direction of the potential bias. A second
limitation is self-selection through the research-interest filter, which
narrows the population further inside the survey.

# Key concepts and operationalisation

The main predictor is researchers' religiosity: an additive index from 0 to
8, an interval-level variable assembled from eight items of different
formats. In this project I split it into two subscales, belief and
practice, both continuous on a 0–1 range.

The first outcome is the author's personal opinion on secularization, a
binary nominal variable, a property of the author. The second outcome is
the conclusion of the publication on secularization, also binary nominal, a
property of the article, produced by manual coding.

Controls: methodology (nominal, three categories), religious tradition
studied (nominal), geographical context (nominal), scholarly influence as
the log of citations and the h-index (continuous), denomination (nominal),
gender (binary), age (continuous), discipline (nominal).

The religiosity scale comes from ESS instruments and from Billiet and Voas
— a validated item set. It includes self-rated religiosity (0–3), four
binary items on belief in heaven, hell, life after death, and God, a
detailed belief-in-God item (0–4), prayer frequency (0–5), and service
attendance (0–6). All items are normalised to 0–1 and summed into a 0–8
score.

**Factor structure and measurement quality.** I checked dimensionality
with parallel analysis: the data retain one component, which accounts for
71 per cent of total variance. Reliability is high: Cronbach's alpha 0.94
for the full scale, 0.93 for belief, and 0.84 for practice. By these
criteria the scale is unidimensional and internally consistent. There is a
measurement-theory subtlety here: technically the score is an index built
by summation, but psychometrically it behaves as a reflective
unidimensional scale, with a single latent construct of religiosity behind
the items. This project tested whether that construct splits into belief
and practice. The data do not separate them: the subscales correlate at
0.83.

**Reflection on construct validity.** The main limitation is the cultural
anchoring of the belief items. Heaven, hell, and belief in God are a
Christian and broadly theistic frame that travels poorly to non-theistic
traditions. Among the studied communities there is Buddhism, Hinduism, and
non-religious groups, and for researchers with such a background the belief
items may underestimate their religiosity or measure something else. The
practice items — prayer and service attendance — travel better, though
"service" presumes a congregational religion. Self-rated religiosity stands
apart, since it captures subjective identity rather than belief or
behaviour. For the purposes of this study, where the religiosity of a
mostly Western group of scholars is what matters, the scale fits, but its
Western-Christian slant is worth keeping in mind.

# Outcomes: operationalisation and critique of wording

Publication conclusions are coded dichotomously: supports secularization or
not. The binary format flattens a position that is more of a continuum,
which the authors acknowledge, explaining the choice as driven by
comparability across papers. Manual coding adds an element of subjectivity.

Author opinion is measured with a single binary question. The wording:
among scholars engaged in debates about secularization, many argue that the
process of secularization manifests as a general decline in religious
beliefs and practices; regardless of the results of your own research, do
you agree with this statement? The clause about independence from results
is well placed — it tries to separate personal opinion from findings. The
weakness is that a complex, graded belief is reduced to a single binary
item, and the nuance of the position disappears. In my view an ordinal
agreement scale would have been preferable.

# Hypotheses and handling of missings

My analysis compares the effects of belief and practice on the two
outcomes in logistic models with clustering by author. Separately, both
axes significantly reduce support for secularization on both outcomes. In
the joint model, practice survives for opinion and belief survives for
publication. But a direct test of coefficient equality shows nothing,
because of the high correlation between the two. The substantive conclusion
is that the choice of measurement shapes the result, and the data are not
always able to separate two ways of measuring the same thing.

On missings, my main analysis runs on complete cases. Religiosity is
missing for 15.8 per cent of cases, and because that missingness is
plausibly tied to religiosity itself, imputation under a missing-at-random
assumption does not fully solve the problem.

# Libraries

```{r libraries}
library(haven)
library(dplyr)
library(psych)
library(diptest)
library(sandwich)
library(car)
library(marginaleffects)
library(ggplot2)
```

```{r helpers, include=FALSE}
alpha  <- psych::alpha
recode <- dplyr::recode
select <- dplyr::select
filter <- dplyr::filter
```

# Data and variables

Path to the data folder.

```{r paths}
base <- "/Users/nikitaobraztsov/Downloads/OSF Storage Archive"
path_fa  <- file.path(base, "factor analysis", "factor_analysis.dta")
path_cln <- file.path(base, "main analysis",   "cleaned_df.dta")
```

I rescale the eight items to 0–1, because they have different ranges and
without rescaling an item with a wide range would weigh more in the sum
than a short one. Dividing by the maximum and subtracting one for binary
items follows what the authors themselves did.

```{r recode-fa}
fa <- read_dta(path_fa)

fa <- fa %>% mutate(
  n_self   = rlgs / 3,          # self-rated religiosity (0-3)
  n_attend = attendance / 6,    # service attendance         [practice]
  n_pray   = pray_freq / 5,     # prayer frequency           [practice]
  n_godD   = blv_god / 4,       # belief in God, detailed    [belief]
  n_hell   = hell_e - 1,        # belief in hell             [belief]
  n_heaven = heaven_e - 1,      # belief in heaven           [belief]
  n_after  = afterdeath_e - 1   # belief in life after death [belief]
)
```

I build three things from the items, because I want to compare belief and
practice as separate predictors. Belief is the mean of five items on God
and the afterlife. Practice is the mean of two items on attendance and
prayer. The overall score is the sum of all eight. I use the mean so that
both parts sit on a 0–1 scale and their effects are comparable. The values
3.22 and 2.94 match Table 2 of the paper, which confirms I built the scale
correctly.

```{r subscales}
belief_items <- c("n_godD","n_hell","n_heaven","n_after")
prac_items   <- c("n_attend","n_pray")
items8       <- c("n_self", prac_items, belief_items)

fa <- fa %>% mutate(
  belief   = rowMeans(across(all_of(belief_items))),   # 0-1
  practice = rowMeans(across(all_of(prac_items))),     # 0-1
  self01   = n_self,                                   # 0-1
  relig08  = rowSums(across(all_of(items8)))           # 0-8
)

cat(sprintf("relig08: mean=%.2f sd=%.2f, missing %.1f%%\n",
            mean(fa$relig08, na.rm=TRUE), sd(fa$relig08, na.rm=TRUE),
            mean(is.na(fa$relig08))*100))
```

I join the subscales to the article-level data, because the models work at
the article level while belief and practice are measured at the author
level. The `cleaned_df` file already holds the outcomes and controls,
recoded by the authors, so I take them as they are. At the end I keep only
complete cases, so all models run on the same sample.

```{r merge}
cl <- read_dta(path_cln)

d <- cl %>%
  select(-any_of("relig08")) %>%
  left_join(select(fa, ResponseID, belief, practice, self01, relig08),
            by = "ResponseID") %>%
  mutate(relig01 = relig08 / 8,
         across(c(method_1, focusrel2, area3, rel_denomin, gndr, accadem_field),
                as_factor))

vars_model <- c("belief","practice","relig01","quality_ln","cent_age",
                "method_1","focusrel2","area3","rel_denomin","gndr","accadem_field")
d_cc <- d %>% filter(if_all(all_of(vars_model), ~ !is.na(.)))

cat(sprintf("All: %d articles, %d authors. In models: %d articles, %d authors.\n",
            nrow(d), n_distinct(d$ResponseID),
            nrow(d_cc), n_distinct(d_cc$ResponseID)))
```

# Descriptive overview

Before the analysis I look at the composition of the sample. The dataset
has 949 articles by 703 authors, and some authors wrote more than one
article, which is why I cluster errors by author later. Below are the
distributions at the article level and at the author level.

```{r freq-fn, include=FALSE}
freq <- function(x){
  x   <- haven::as_factor(x)
  tab <- as.data.frame(table(x)); names(tab) <- c("category","n")
  tab$`%` <- round(100 * tab$n / sum(tab$n), 1)
  tab
}
```

```{r descriptives}
da <- distinct(d, ResponseID, .keep_all = TRUE)   # one row per author

freq(d$outcome_1)      # publication conclusion
freq(d$method_1)       # methodology
freq(da$opinion_1)     # author's personal opinion
freq(da$rel_denomin)   # denomination
freq(da$accadem_field) # discipline
freq(da$gndr)          # gender

cat(sprintf("Age: mean=%.1f sd=%.1f (%.0f-%.0f)\n",
            mean(da$age, na.rm=TRUE), sd(da$age, na.rm=TRUE),
            min(da$age, na.rm=TRUE), max(da$age, na.rm=TRUE)))
```

Publication conclusions split almost evenly (46 per cent find
secularization, 54 do not). Author opinion leans toward secularization (57
against 43). The sample is 72 per cent male, mean age 51, about half the
authors have no denomination, and sociologists dominate.

# Scale properties

Before running regressions I check whether the eight items can be summed
into one score at all.

I check the shape of the distribution, because the regression treats the
score as continuous and that only makes sense if values are spread
evenly. The distribution is bimodal: p below 0.0001, BC coefficient 0.72.
The sample splits into a secular edge at zero and a religious edge at the
top, with an empty middle. So the religiosity effect later is essentially a
contrast between two edges.

```{r dip-test}
x <- na.omit(fa$relig08)
d.test <- dip.test(x)
BC <- (skew(x)^2 + 1) / (kurtosi(x) + 3*(length(x)-1)^2 /
                            ((length(x)-2)*(length(x)-3)))

cat(sprintf("dip p=%.4f | BC=%.2f | at zero (0-1): %.0f%% | at top (6-8): %.0f%%\n",
            d.test$p.value, BC, mean(x<=1)*100, mean(x>=6)*100))

hist(x, breaks = 0:8, col = "grey80",
     main = "Religiosity scale (0-8)", xlab = "")
```

I check whether a single dimension sits behind the eight items, because
the composite score is only justified in that case. Parallel analysis of
components compares the data with random noise and retains one component,
which takes 71 per cent of total variance. I also look at what would happen
with two factors: the second factor collects belief in hell, heaven, and
the afterlife. So the data split along the line of supernatural belief.

```{r parallel-analysis}
D <- fa %>% select(all_of(items8)) %>% na.omit()

fa.parallel(D, fa = "pc", main = "Parallel analysis")

pc1 <- principal(D, nfactors = 1)
cat(sprintf("One component takes %.0f%% of variance.\n\n",
            pc1$Vaccounted["Proportion Var", 1] * 100))

pc2 <- principal(D, nfactors = 2, rotate = "oblimin")
print(pc2$loadings, cutoff = 0.30)
```

Now Cronbach's alpha is worth reporting, because summing items into a
score is only defensible when they agree. Alpha is high everywhere: 0.94
for the full scale, 0.93 for belief, 0.84 for practice. Both the composite
and the two subscales are internally reliable.

```{r reliability}
cat(sprintf("alpha: full=%.2f  belief=%.2f  practice=%.2f\n",
            alpha(fa[items8])$total$raw_alpha,
            alpha(fa[belief_items])$total$raw_alpha,
            alpha(fa[prac_items])$total$raw_alpha))
```

I look at the correlation between belief and practice, because it tells me
in advance whether they can be separated in a single model. The
correlation is 0.83, which is very high: the items overlap heavily and
separating their effects will be difficult.

```{r correlation}
cat(sprintf("Belief ~ practice correlation: r=%.2f\n",
            cor(fa$belief, fa$practice, use = "complete.obs")))
```

# Models

I fit logistic regressions here, because both outcomes are binary: does the
author support secularization or not. The unit of analysis is the article,
and I cluster errors by author, because articles by the same person are not
independent. I report effects as percentage-point changes in probability
via marginal effects, which are easier to read than logit coefficients. I
rescaled the composite score to 0–1 so its effect is comparable with belief
and practice. For each outcome I run four models: composite score, belief
alone, practice alone, and both together.

```{r helper-ame, include=FALSE}
controls <- paste("method_1 + quality_ln + focusrel2 + area3 +",
                  "rel_denomin + cent_age + gndr + accadem_field")

ame <- function(model, v){
  s <- avg_slopes(model, variables = v, vcov = ~ResponseID)
  data.frame(term = s$term,
             AME  = round(s$estimate, 3),
             p    = round(s$p.value, 3))
}
```

```{r opinion-models}
op_full <- glm(as.formula(paste("opinion_1 ~ relig01 +", controls)),
               d_cc, family = binomial)
op_bel  <- glm(as.formula(paste("opinion_1 ~ belief +", controls)),
               d_cc, family = binomial)
op_prac <- glm(as.formula(paste("opinion_1 ~ practice +", controls)),
               d_cc, family = binomial)
op_both <- glm(as.formula(paste("opinion_1 ~ belief + practice +", controls)),
               d_cc, family = binomial)

ame(op_full, "relig01")
ame(op_bel,  "belief")
ame(op_prac, "practice")
ame(op_both, c("belief","practice"))
```

```{r publication-models}
pub_full <- glm(as.formula(paste("outcome_1 ~ relig01 +", controls)),
                d_cc, family = binomial)
pub_bel  <- glm(as.formula(paste("outcome_1 ~ belief +", controls)),
                d_cc, family = binomial)
pub_prac <- glm(as.formula(paste("outcome_1 ~ practice +", controls)),
                d_cc, family = binomial)
pub_both <- glm(as.formula(paste("outcome_1 ~ belief + practice +", controls)),
                d_cc, family = binomial)

ame(pub_full, "relig01")
ame(pub_bel,  "belief")
ame(pub_prac, "practice")
ame(pub_both, c("belief","practice"))
```

Separately, both belief and practice significantly reduce support for
secularization on both outcomes. In the joint model, practice stays
significant for opinion and belief drops to zero. For publications it is
the other way around: belief stays and practice drops to zero. At first
glance this looks like two different lines: opinion runs on practice,
publications run on belief.

# Testing the difference

A significant predictor in a joint model alongside a non-significant one
does not by itself mean the two are different. So I test the difference
directly, using a linear hypothesis on the equality of the belief and
practice coefficients. The test gives p around 0.36 and 0.35 for the two
outcomes: the difference is not significant. VIF around 4.4 shows why.
Belief and practice overlap heavily, and the data simply lack the spread to
attribute the effect confidently to one of them.

```{r lh-opinion}
linearHypothesis(op_both, "belief = practice",
                 vcov. = vcovCL(op_both, cluster = ~ResponseID))
```

```{r lh-publication}
linearHypothesis(pub_both, "belief = practice",
                 vcov. = vcovCL(pub_both, cluster = ~ResponseID))
vif(pub_both)[c("belief","practice"), ]
```

# Robustness

I check the result on the subsample of quantitative articles, where
religiosity is measured in more standard ways and depends less on
interpretation. The lead role of belief for publications is even stronger
there (−0.30). Separately I recompute opinion on one observation per
author, because opinion is a property of the person, while the main model
repeats it as many times as the author has articles. At the pure author
level the direction of the subscales is the same, so the result is not an
artefact.

```{r robustness-quant}
quant <- d_cc %>% filter(method_1 == "Quantitative") %>% droplevels()
pub_q <- glm(outcome_1 ~ belief + practice + quality_ln + focusrel2 +
               area3 + rel_denomin + cent_age + gndr + accadem_field,
             quant, family = binomial)
cat("Quantitative articles, publication conclusion:\n")
ame(pub_q, c("belief","practice"))
```

```{r robustness-author}
authors <- distinct(d, ResponseID, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  filter(!is.na(opinion_1), !is.na(belief), !is.na(practice))
op_auth <- glm(opinion_1 ~ belief + practice + rel_denomin + gndr + cent_age,
               authors, family = binomial)
cat("\nOpinion, author level:\n")
ame(op_auth, c("belief","practice"))
```

# Plot

Effects of belief and practice on one plot. The point is the estimate, the
segment is the confidence interval, and the vertical line at zero is the
significance threshold. In separate models both axes are significant; in
the joint model practice survives for opinion and belief survives for
publications. The belief and practice intervals overlap considerably, which
is exactly why the equality test fails.

```{r plot, fig.height=5}
one <- function(model, v, spec, outcome){
  s <- avg_slopes(model, variables = v, vcov = ~ResponseID)
  data.frame(outcome, spec, term = s$term,
             est = s$estimate, lo = s$conf.low, hi = s$conf.high)
}
plotdf <- rbind(
  one(op_bel,  "belief",               "belief alone",    "Opinion"),
  one(op_prac, "practice",             "practice alone",  "Opinion"),
  one(op_both, c("belief","practice"), "joint",           "Opinion"),
  one(pub_bel, "belief",               "belief alone",    "Publications"),
  one(pub_prac,"practice",             "practice alone",  "Publications"),
  one(pub_both,c("belief","practice"), "joint",           "Publications")
)
plotdf$term <- ifelse(plotdf$term == "belief", "belief", "practice")

ggplot(plotdf, aes(est, spec, color = term)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_point(position = position_dodge(0.4), size = 2.5) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi),
                 position = position_dodge(0.4), height = 0.2) +
  facet_wrap(~outcome) +
  labs(x = "Effect on probability of supporting secularization (0 -> 1 shift)",
       y = NULL, color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

# Conclusion

The composite religiosity score contains two parts, belief and practice,
and I tried to see which of them drives the bias in research. The scale
turned out to be bimodal in shape, unidimensional in structure, and
reliable in internal consistency, so summing the items into a score is
defensible on these data. Separately, both belief and practice reduce
support for secularization. I could not separate their contributions in
the joint model: they are too similar, correlated at 0.83, and the
equality test shows nothing. The apparent negative result is the
substantive one. How you choose to measure religiosity shapes what you
find, and the data are not always able to distinguish two ways of
measuring what is, in effect, one thing. For a paper that itself studies
bias in science, this matters: the instrument used to measure researchers'
religiosity inherits the same dependence on measurement choice as the
subject of their debate.
